articles.title: Universal Still Plans Overseas Release for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Documentary Despite Mogul’s Legal Threats
articles.summary: Contrary to a recent report, Universal is moving forward as planned with the international release of Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” sources familiar with the project told Variety.
body: After the documentary premiered at the Venice Film Festival, the tech mogul began posting comments on X, calling the doc “a hit piece,” though it was not clear whether he had seen the film.

Musk asserted that Gibney had “just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind).” Among the interviews featured in Gibney’s film is one with Ashley St. Clair, a MAGA influencer who had a child with Musk. The documentary portrays a text exchange between the two about the 2024 presidential election.
Musk’s attorney Alex Spiro threatened to file a defamation lawsuit before the film’s release in October, pointing to Musk’s texts with St. Clair.

Variety critic Owen Gleiberman wrote in his review of “Musk” in Venice, “Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers … Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot,” Universal and Gibney had no comment.

articles.title: Nick Kroll Delivers Heartfelt Appeal for Productions to Shoot in L.A.: ‘It Will Bring Life Back’ to the City
articles.summary: Nick Kroll said upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent,” which he co-created and stars in, is a “love letter” to Los Angeles — and he expressed hope that a “thriving” entertainment production community will bring “vitality” to the city.
body: He co-created “A Hundred Percent” with his friend Gabe Liedman (creator of “Q-Force” and showrunner of the first season of “PEN15”), and stars in the show alongside Sam Richardson, Jason Mantzoukas and Vanessa Bayer, with Diane Lane joining the cast in a recurring role.

“We genuinely felt like it was a love letter to the city that we live in. And we really, honestly, have the best crew, had the best people, who were in such a happy mood making a show in Los Angeles,” said Kroll, who was interviewed on stage by Angelique Jackson, senior entertainment writer at Variety. “It was an awesome experience, and I’m so grateful to the city for helping make that happen. I hope it continues to grow because I think all of the doldrums that we’ve all been feeling for so many years will hopefully begin to work itself out.”

Kroll continued: “The more that we have a thriving, ongoing shooting community here in Los Angeles, it will bring life back. Not only money, but just like it will bring a vitalization, a vitality to the city that I think I have missed from when I moved here, and like the dream of coming to Hollywood and making things and being around people who are making things.”

articles.title: Battling Misconceptions and Figuring Out Use Cases: Entertainment Leaders Navigate AI’s Place in the Industry
articles.summary: In a world where AI is capturing every conversation, a series of experts is trying to figure out what it actually means for the world of entertainment. “I think the word ‘AI’ is doing too much right now,” says Mira Line, Google’s vice president of technology and society.
body: That comes down to building relationships with creators about how it can be used, including where it fits within the production landscape. Balakrishnan highlighted Netflix’s public framework for how the company uses AI within its production pipeline (on a generative level, for roughly 300 programs ), a model he said “builds trust with the creative community” and gives those members ”a pathway to navigate to drive use cases that are meaningful to the creative process.”

The industry is already landing on other frameworks surrounding AI’s place in the industry, such as the Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute-led “Human Generative Workflows” paper published last month. Lane helped develop the paper, which she said breaks down the use cses in ways that can help AI-backed productions reach a still-elusive goal: being copyrightable.

“We did a whole exercise around tooling and looking at everything from de-noising techniques to fully synthetic characters,” she said. “Let’s start thinking about the vocabulary and breaking it down so it’s not just AI as one big monolithic.”

articles.title: Why stop at Wuthering Heights: House of the Damned? Bring on Mrs Dalloway’s Rampage!
articles.summary: It isn’t just Winnie the Pooh – now the star of Blood & Honey II. Budget shockers are treating any story with expired copyright as ripe for murderous exploitation. It is significant that, at this point in our cultural journey, we have become accustomed to film producers jumping on every single…
body: But if you zoom out even a tiny amount, it all starts to look a little silly. Not because it suggests the paying public has a fondness for inarguably bad horror films based on loose interpretations of recognisable figures, but because it’s missing the bigger picture. In other words, while producers are watching eagerly for the next newly out-of-copyright property to exploit (by the way, Babar the Elephant will enter the public domain in January), there is an entire ocean of public domain work just sitting there to be desecrated.

In which case, you really have to applaud whoever came up with the idea of Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned. Available on digital platforms in three short weeks (on 19 October in fact), it is a remake of Emily Brontë’s classic novel, only scarier. In the film, as far as I am able to tell, Cathy has died and her ghost starts haunting Heathcliff to the point that he starts murdering everyone. Is it any good? All signs point to not really, especially since the trailer contains a shot where Cathy seems to become a zombie so that she can punch through a window and strangle someone to death. But will I watch it? Oh God, try to stop me.

articles.title: ‘Resident Evil’ Racing Toward Healthy Box Office Haul for Zach Cregger’s Reboot
articles.summary: Austin Abrams stars in Sony's latest feature adaptation of the video game franchise, with the new movie becoming the first in the series to impress critics.
body: Resident Evil looks to get off to a running start in its opening weekend at the box office.

A launch of $40 million would give the new Resident Evil the distinction of the highest-grossing opening in the history of the franchise. The series’ previous titles have collectively grossed more than $1.2 billion worldwide.

Hailing from TriStar Pictures, Constantin Film and Davis Film, Resident Evil stars Austin Abrams, Zach Cherry, Kali Reis and Paul Walter Hauser in the story of a medical courier (Abrams) attempting to deliver a precious item in the midst of a deadly viral outbreak in Raccoon City. The movie looks to continue the hot streak for Cregger, whose most recent release was Warner Bros.’ Oscar-winning horror film Weapons, which hit theaters last summer, and before that was his well-received Barbarian.

articles.title: Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Gala and Anime Selections, Featuring Cate Blanchett, Tony Gilroy, ‘Wild Horse Nine’ and ‘Grotesqqque’
articles.summary: The festival’s high-profile sidebar will also showcase new films from Cristian Mungiu, Wayne Wang, Jane Schoenbrun and Yukiko Sode, while its animation program spotlights new work from CloverWorks, Madhouse and DreamWorks.
body: The Tokyo International Film Festival has unveiled the Gala and Animation selections for its 39th edition, bringing a mix of recent festival standouts, star-driven international titles and high-profile Japanese animation to the Japanese capital next month.

The section will also feature several prominent Asian titles, including Japanese filmmaker Sabu’s Taiwan-set Arrested Memory, which stars Ethan Juan and Wayne Wang’s Tokyo-set Diary of a Mad Old Man, starring Lily Franky and Fan Bingbing. The lineup also includes Yukiko Sode’s Cannes standout All the Lovers in the Night, Kazuya Shiraishi’s Bye Bye Love: Detective Is in the Bar and the feature adaptation The Tiger and Her Wings The Movie.

On the animation side, the festival’s 12-title program ranges from major Japanese studio productions to new international work. Among the most buzzy entries is Grotesqqque, an original anthology feature from director Atsushi Nishigori and CloverWorks, the studio behind Spy x Family and Bocchi the Rock!.

articles.title: Marooned Lord Byron statue returns to Hyde Park
articles.summary: The statue was left isolated on a Park Lane traffic island after new roads were built in the 1960s.
body: A statue of the 19th-century poet Lord Byron has been returned to Hyde Park, nearly 70 years after it was isolated on a traffic island when new roads were built through the area in the early 1960s.

The Grade II-listed statue was erected as a national memorial in 1880 after receiving special permission from Queen Victoria. Changes to the Park Lane road layout 80 years later left it inaccessible, leading it to become isolated, neglected and dirty.
The Lord Byron Society launched a campaign to relocate the statue six years ago, arguing it had become neglected.
The move cost more than £400,000, funded by a £230,000 grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional donations.

articles.title: Inde Navarrette: I Didn’t “Want to Make Any Friends” During ‘Obsession’ Shoot to Focus on Film
articles.summary: "It's not of, 'I'm trying to be a dick,'" the actress explained during an onstage conversation with director Curry Barker about Focus Features' horror smash.
body: Inde Navarrette was dead set on prioritizing her work while filming writer-director Curry Barker ‘s horror sensation Obsession.

“There’s a lot of people there on the other side of that camera, and to ask her to make a fool of herself in front of all these people was asking a lot,” Barker said. The director added about his efforts to keep everyone comfortable: “We’d like to keep it playful.”

Navarrette agreed before segueing into a point she wanted to make to any aspiring performers in the crowd. She explained that part of the appeal of working on a set could be the chance to develop close bonds with the cast and crew, but she told herself ahead of time that she would avoid trying to make new friends in order to feel empowered to ask for what she needed during the shoot.

articles.title: ‘When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true’: the incredible journey behind The Cycle of Love
articles.summary: Documentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heart. New Delhi, December 1975.
body: New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.

Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.
